generatedProse.concept-context: Across disciplines, active engagement is the difference between a reader who accepts a summary of an idea and one who asks what evidence it rests on. A settled-sounding claim, that something simply works, say, invites an active reader to ask how it was tested, in what conditions, and against what alternative. Opening up that discussion, rather than taking the summary as final, is the everyday habit of a critical student in any field.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students reading the same passage, which states an idea as though it were settled fact.

Student A reads it, accepts the idea, and writes it into his notes as a fact to use later. The point is captured, but Student A has taken the author's word for it, with no sense of the evidence behind the claim or the debate around it. This is passive engagement.

Student B pauses on the words that make it sound settled. Is this really agreed? She checks what the claim rests on, finds other sources and a disagreement, and sees the field is still arguing. The idea goes into her notes as a position to weigh, not a fact to repeat. This is active engagement: she has opened up the discourse.

Both students read the passage. Only Student B treated it as something to question.
generatedProse.summary: Being critical becomes real work when you engage with a source actively: questioning its claim, checking the evidence, and bringing in other voices rather than accepting a single summary. You can now tell active engagement from passive and choose an active move when a claim sounds settled. The next lesson gives you the language to describe these moves.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Student B do that opened up the discourse around the source?

items.text: She found other sources and a disagreement, and saw the field was still arguing.
She accepted the idea because the passage stated it clearly.
She read the passage more slowly than Student A did.
She copied the claim into her notes word for word.

feedback.correct: That's right. Bringing in other sources and a disagreement turned a single claim into a live debate.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that brought in other evidence or views, rather than accepting or copying the claim.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B opened up the discourse by finding other sources and a disagreement. Accepting, re-reading or copying all leave the single claim as the last word.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
